lesson_title: One Year, Three Photographs: Company Statements and the Cash Flow
hook_text: The company made R394 200 profit. Its bank balance went DOWN. Both numbers are true.
clip_script: A family runs a tuck shop, and in December three questions get asked around the table. How did we do this year? That's the income statement — a video of the whole year, ending on one number: profit of R394 200. What do we have now? That's the balance sheet — a photograph at midnight on the last day, everything owned on one side, everyone with a claim on the other, both sides at R3 750 000. And then the grade 12 question: where is the CASH? Because here's the strange part — the video says almost four hundred thousand profit, but the tin has LESS money than last year. Both true. Profit counts a sale the moment it happens, even if the customer pays next month. It spreads the cost of the fridge over years. Cash counts only rands actually moving. The cash flow statement is the bridge: trading put in two hundred and ninety-seven thousand, buying equipment took out four hundred and seventy, new shares and the loan brought back one hundred and forty. Net effect: the tin is down thirty-three thousand — and when your statement lands exactly on the balance sheet's cash figure, you know every line was true. Profitable AND shrinking cash: the company invested in its own future. That's the story the numbers tell.
visual_style: A film reel, a framed photograph and a rope bridge rendered side by side; rand notes flowing across the bridge in three labelled streams, the cash tin's level falling as an equipment crate lands, the final balance clicking into the photograph.
pacing: Three-question build, hard stop on the paradox, steady bridge walk, clean landing.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and build all three statements until they balance to the rand.
